title: Choir singers' hearts beat together
hook: When a choir sings together, the singers' heart rates rise and fall together.
peek: A Swedish study in 2013 wired up young choir singers and found their heart rates speeding up and slowing down in step as they sang. The link is breathing: singing sets the rhythm of every breath, and the heart follows.
lede: In 2013 a team at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden attached heart monitors to a group of 18-year-old singers and asked them to sing together. As the music went on, the singers' heart rates began rising and falling together. The study was small, but the reason it found is simple: in a choir, the music decides when everyone breathes.

bullets.text: The study, led by Björn Vickhoff and published in Frontiers in Psychology, had the singers hum a single note, sing a hymn and chant a slow mantra. Each task produced a different pattern of heart rate, and the patterns lined up across the group.

The heart speeds up a little as we breathe in and slows as we breathe out, a normal rhythm called heart rate variability. Singing stretches out each exhale, so when a choir breathes at the same moments, their heart rates swing together too.

The strongest effect came from the slow mantra, with long phrases and regular breaths. The researchers compared it to the effect of slow, guided breathing exercises, and suggested the steady rhythm of singing may be part of why people find it calming.
